https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/j.text: Organisers submitted more than 100 proposed routes to authorities in Oradea, but all were rejected Photograph: Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights View image in fullscreen Organisers submitted more than 100 proposed routes to authorities in Oradea, but all were rejected Photograph: Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights Romania Pride organisers vow to march in Romanian city that has blocked event four years in a row Oradea is only major city in EU where local authorities have repeatedly blocked Pride plans Ashifa Kassam European community affairs correspondent Thu 23 Jul 2026 04.36 EDT Last modified on Thu 23 Jul 2026 21.30 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Campaigners in a Romanian city have vowed to go ahead with a Pride march after local authorities denied permission for the fourth consecutive year. Since 2023, campaigners in the western city of Oradea, which has a population of about 180,000, have sought permission to hold Pride events. However, each year they have faced opposition, making Oradea the only major city in the EU where local authorities have repeatedly blocked Pride marches. “Every year the local authorities have managed to find legal or technical excuses to ban Oradea Pride events,” said Iulian Dițiu, the co-founder and president of Ark Oradea, the local organiser of Pride. In 2024, they were told none of the city’s parks were available at the times requested, he said. The following year, campaigners submitted 12 potential routes for the march, only to be told that none was suitable. In the run-up to Saturday’s proposed march, organisers submitted more than 100 possible routes. On Wednesday, the city authorities said none of them was viable because they clashed with other events or public infrastructure works. The mayor, who belongs to a party that describes itself as liberal, conservative and Christian democratic, did not respond to a request for comment from the Guardian. Dițiu said the repeated refusals sent a broader message. “It feels like the message that they are trying to send our way is that we’re not welcome here,” he said. “They have never said out loud that they are banning Pride for LGBT reasons. They’re always hiding behind technical reasons.” The dispute has attracted growing international attention. More than 152 organisations from 30 countries have signed a statement calling on officials to allow the march to take place “in complete safety” and in line with EU law. “After four consecutive years in which the Pride march has been unable to take place, there can be no question of administrative or logistical difficulties,” the statement said. “When an authority consistently prevents a community from assembling peacefully, a principle that concerns all citizens is undermined.” Their appeal, delivered recently to the local administration in Oradea, drew comparisons between Oradea and Budapest, where Hungary’s former prime minister Viktor Orbán and his rightwing populist movement had sought to ban Pride events. “In recent years, the restriction of Pride marches has become, in several European states, an indicator of democratic backsliding and the weakening of the rule of law,” the statement said. Dițiu said organisers intended to proceed with the march on Saturday despite the lack of official permission, repeating last year’s approach. In 2025, between 500 and 600 people attended an unauthorised march, with nine participants later fined the equivalent of about €4,000 (£3,420) he said. This time representatives from several diplomatic missions have said they will take part, along with Romania’s ombudsman, he added. Dițiu described the situation as both “encouraging and disappointing”. “The institutions that are supposed to protect the rights of every community are trying to use our community as a scapegoat. But many more people are behind us. Many more people understand what the stakes are,” he said. “This is not an LGBT issue. This is a democratic issue. It’s about the freedom to public assembly. And if the local LGBT community here in Oradea can be denied this basic human right without any repercussion, it can happen pretty much anywhere in Europe, for pretty much any community.” Explore more on these topics Romania Pride LGBTQ+ rights Europe Human rights news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.dailystar.co.uk/news/latest-.text: An explosive-laden drone found at at a major airport in Germany could have belonged to the Russian government, according to US officials. The drone, which reportedly contained the explosive substance Semtex, was discovered in a secure area close to a Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft on August 4, prompting the airport to close for the night. Reports state that the drone may have actually struck the plane near its fuel tank, although it failed to detonate. One official told the German news outlet BILD: “Had the drone exploded there, it would have caused an inferno .” The impact damaged the drone and left fragments on the aircraft’s wing. It then fell to the ground, where it apparently remained in emergency mode for around four hours before a bus driver reportedly stepped on it and alerted airport security. Investigators recovered DNA from the device which, according to BILD, matches evidence found after an incendiary parcel caught fire at DHL’s Leipzig logistics centre on July 20, 2024. That earlier parcel was due to be loaded onto a DHL aircraft but ignited on the ground because the flight had been delayed. Five men are now standing trial in Lithuania accused of sending four incendiary parcels across Europe. Eurojust previously said 22 suspects identified over the parcel-bomb campaign were believed to have acted on behalf of Russia ’s GRU military intelligence service. The DNA has not yet been linked to any specific, but it has reportedly been linked to an unknowwn individual in Lithuania. The device was reportedly equipped with explosives, two SIM cards and a release mechanism. German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt described the discovery as “a new level of danger” and “a new threat scenario”, but did not publicly blame Russia. German investigators are examining whether a foreign state was involved. Authorities are also looking into a second unidentified object which reportedly struck another cargo plane after it aborted its landing because of the airport closure. The aircraft suffered minor damage and landed safely elsewhere. The alleged Russian connection comes amid warnings that Vladimir Putin could seek to test NATO’s resolve through cyberattacks, sabotage or a limited incursion into an allied country. However, there is currently no publicly available evidence that Putin personally ordered the drone to be sent. Germany’s Federal Criminal Police Office is believed to be investigating the incident.

Photograph: Kevin Carter/Getty Images US supreme court US supreme court lifts restrictions on controversial voter database Trump and officials claimed it combats voting by noncitizens but critics said it could disenfranchise eligible voters Guardian staff and agencies Fri 25 Sep 2026 11.52 EDT Last modified on Fri 25 Sep 2026 11.55 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The US supreme court has lifted restrictions on a controversial federal database of voters as Donald Trump seeks to impose tougher restrictions on voting ahead of November’s midterm elections. While the president and his officials have claimed the expanded database aims to combat voting by noncitizens, critics contend it could disenfranchise eligible voters. The justices granted a request from the Trump administration on Friday ⁠to block a judge’s order which ⁠had stopped state officials from using ​social security numbers and other information to conduct sweeping checks of the citizenship status of registered voters against federal records.
